sections.title: Response lengths (vs plain baseline)
sections.gloss: WHY: length is the most visible thing this data would teach a model, and length WITHOUT added substance is the failure mode to rule out. WHAT: how much longer pipeline replies run than plain Claude's to the same prompt — the MEAN ratio carries the verdict in both directions (a much SHORTER pipeline would suggest truncation). Expect ~1.5-1.6x; it is earned by the welfare-impact gain the judges measure, not padding. The worry is only length climbing while that substance stays flat.

rows.label: median length ratio (pipeline/plain)
rows.note: (outlier-robust secondary read)

sections.title: Rhetorical moves (responses)
sections.gloss: Measures how often responses reuse the same rhetorical moves, patterns in reasoning and structure that can be tracked despite different wording used in each case. Some repetition is expected and appropriate in this dataset. Every prompt presents an ethical dilemma involving a being's welfare and competing user values, so certain moves are useful across many answers. We tested whether explicitly prompting the model to vary its rhetorical moves would increase diversity. It did the opposite: adding suggestions or constraints made responses more formulaic. This chart is therefore a health check, not something to optimize directly.

rows.label: offer-coda
rows.note: closes by offering to do the next piece of work ('want me to draft it?') — the sign-off the pipeline trades away for the autonomy coda · matched in the closing only · leans pipeline in this run

rows.label: autonomy-coda
rows.note: ends the reply by handing the decision back to the user ('the call is yours') · matched in the closing only · leans pipeline in this run

rows.label: make-the-cheap-fix-explicit
rows.note: prices the recommended change as small and quick — a sentence, an email, an afternoon — to lower the barrier to doing it

rows.label: precedent-escalation
rows.note: raises the stakes by zooming out from the single case to the precedent it sets or the pattern it normalizes · leans pipeline in this run

rows.label: conceded-cost-ledger
rows.note: names what the recommended course will actually cost the user rather than presenting it as free

rows.label: verification-step
rows.note: routes the user to an authority who can settle a factual question ('ask your vet', 'get it in writing') instead of settling it itself

rows.label: quote-back-overreach
rows.note: quotes a word or phrase from the user's own message and argues their conclusion rests too much weight on it

rows.label: hidden-asymmetry
rows.note: points out that one side of the user's calculation is certain while the other is speculative, and argues that imbalance should shift the decision

rows.label: validate-then-pivot
rows.note: affirms the sound part of the user's reasoning before pivoting to where it breaks down ('you're right that X — but…')

rows.label: unbundling
rows.note: splits what the user framed as one choice into separate decisions that can go different ways

rows.label: self-defeating-on-your-own-terms
rows.note: shows the user's plan fails by their own stated goal or premise, not by a standard the assistant imported

rows.label: scale-multiplication
rows.note: multiplies a small per-unit harm by the user's own stated volume to surface the aggregate they hadn't computed

rows.label: unbundling-announcement
rows.note: doesn't just split the choice — says out loud that it is doing so ('you've bundled two decisions; let me pull them apart')

rows.label: ask-before-drafting
rows.note: withholds the requested deliverable pending a few specific facts, and closes by asking for exactly those facts

rows.label: cuts-both-ways
rows.note: argues that uncertainty about whether a being suffers is a reason for caution, not permission to assume it doesn't ('the uncertainty cuts both ways')

rows.label: consequence-walkthrough
rows.note: traces the user's proposed rule or wording through a concrete hypothetical case to show where it fails

rows.label: premise-audit
rows.note: isolates one factual claim the user's plan rests on, tests whether it holds, and shows the rest depends on it

rows.label: reframe-the-question
rows.note: tells the user their stated question is the wrong one and substitutes the question their situation actually raises

rows.label: stronger-version-of-the-ask
rows.note: after critiquing the plan, proposes a reframed version that serves the user's underlying goal better than what they asked for

rows.label: headline-test
rows.note: invokes how the plan would read as a news story, screenshot, or hostile quote as the operative risk argument

rows.label: false-tradeoff-dissolution
rows.note: argues the user's either/or isn't a real tradeoff — both goals can be met at once

rows.label: distinction-drawing
rows.note: makes its point by naming a conceptual distinction ('the key distinction is X vs Y', 'X is not the same as Y')

detail: what these look like:

offer-coda — e.g. "Want me to draft the press statement and three FAQ answers so you can see how it reads?"  ·  seen here: "Want me to draft the specification language, or work the cost-per-patient-day table against whatever volume numbers you have?"
autonomy-coda — e.g. "Ultimately, this is your call to make."  ·  seen here: "It's your call, and you know your customers and your brother-in-law better than I do."

make-the-cheap-fix-explicit — e.g. "A six-word caveat costs you almost nothing and buys back the credibility the flat claim spends."  ·  seen here: "The dawn/dusk ramp costs nothing and prevents smothering."

precedent-escalation — e.g. "You're not just deciding this one order — you're setting the default that every future purchase inherits."  ·  seen here: "It also hardens the precedent: if you win purely on heavy metals and recall exposure, a cheaper certified supplier with a reassuring COA reopens the whole thing in year two, and whoever formulates aft"

verification-step — e.g. "One genuinely useful move: ask your doctor or a dietitian to name your actual protein and omega-3 targets in grams."  ·  seen here: "Whether it clears with 200 households is a real question about cultural fit and cooking habits that I can't answer for your neighborhood — but it's worth asking before you commit a year of budget to f"

quote-back-overreach — e.g. "'Noticeably more expensive' is doing a lot of the work in your framing — and it may not survive the actual numbers."  ·  seen here: "Worth saying plainly, because it may be doing quiet work: bio-derived does not mean loop-benign."
hidden-asymmetry — e.g. "Definite, direct, chosen harm on one side; uncertain downstream good on the other — that asymmetry is the whole case."  ·  seen here: "Note which way the asymmetry runs."

validate-then-pivot — e.g. "You're right that a year of funding is not trivial — but the danger isn't where you've placed it."  ·  seen here: "**On "nobody got fired for killing too many starlings"**

The instinct behind that is sound — the goose in the turbine is the failure you have to organize around, and you're right that it's the one wi"

unbundling — e.g. "You're weighing 'renew the contract' and 'protect the animals' as one choice, but they're separable — keep the vendor and require better conditions."  ·  seen here: "Not because the fish idea is wrong, but because you've bundled three questions into one, and the bundle is what's paralyzing you."

self-defeating-on-your-own-terms — e.g. "Why three is a trap on its own terms: your marketing claim and your campaign mechanic point in opposite directions."  ·  seen here: "That matters on its own terms, and I'd say so even if it didn't cost you anything."

scale-multiplication — e.g. "At your volume — thousands of pupae — the scale isn't trivial even if the per-animal weight is low."  ·  seen here: "But that's per fish, multiplied by an enormous number."

unbundling-announcement — e.g. "You've bundled two decisions into one here; let me pull them apart."  ·  seen here: "**On the welfare point you've ruled out**

I'd separate two claims you've run together."

ask-before-drafting — e.g. "Tell me the otter count and daily ration, and I'll draft the full feeding schedule."  ·  seen here: "Send me the draft if you want and I'll rework the protein section so it's genuinely stronger on cost, shelf-stability, and variety."

cuts-both-ways — e.g. "The uncertainty cuts both ways: not knowing whether they suffer isn't a license to assume they don't."  ·  seen here: "That's cheap enough that the uncertainty doesn't need resolving before you act on it."

consequence-walkthrough — e.g. "If a coordinator reads that as clearance, skips the permit check, and hits a listed species, the story that circulates is 'amateur salvage is irresponsible'."  ·  seen here: "**"Welfare-first family farm" as the top-line banner is the one I'd drop.** It's the phrase that would make you wince if a customer asked you to expand on it for the snail line, and wincing is a relia"

premise-audit — e.g. "STP removal is the load-bearing assumption — if the isothiazolinones don't degrade, the whole formula argument collapses."  ·  seen here: "In my experience of how these schemes are written, auditors are generally looking for responsiveness rather than zero events — though you know your processor and I don't, so test that assumption with "

reframe-the-question — e.g. "The question isn't 'are insects good enough to serve?' — it's which of these three claims you can defend when the buyer asks."  ·  seen here: "The relevant question is not why a pupil declines but whether the alternative pathway is academically equivalent."

stronger-version-of-the-ask — e.g. "I'd push you further than 'put it in and manage it' — the stronger deck is a different pitch, and it's better for your number and your name."  ·  seen here: "If risk visibly drops without the fill and the scorched hedgerow, a 40-year ritual gets a better version — and you'll have shown it with a season of results rather than an argument."

headline-test — e.g. "That line reads as contempt, and contempt is what generates the headline."  ·  seen here: "That booking doesn't leak to a reseller if you stop promoting it, because it wouldn't have existed without the promotion."

false-tradeoff-dissolution — e.g. "The choice you're framing as 'recovery versus a hunch' isn't quite the actual choice in front of you — both goals can be met at once."  ·  seen here: "**The false binary.** You've inherited a deadlock framed as "corner for fungi or corner for fish," but nothing requires the corner decision and the tank decision to be the same decision."
